evidenceAudit.scope: Adults with HHS or mixed DKA–HHS. Haemodynamically unstable patients are resuscitated first (ICU). Verified against SDCPG 2021 pp. 75–79 and the 2024 consensus.
findings: Every dose, threshold and timing was checked against the cited source section on 12 Oct 2026.
Normal values are typical adult reference ranges; laboratories differ.
unverifiedSections: Local formulary availability and hospital protocol adoption

pathophysiology.summary: HHS is severe hyperglycaemia, hyperosmolality and dehydration without significant ketoacidosis. There is enough insulin to stop ketogenesis but not enough to control glucose, so osmotic diuresis runs for days and the fluid deficit is huge.
keyMechanisms: Relative insulin deficiency plus counter-regulatory hormones: hepatic glucose output rises and uptake falls, so glucose climbs above 30 mmol/L.
Osmotic diuresis: water and electrolytes are lost over days; SDCPG notes the fluid deficit is often over 8 L.
Hyperosmolality: water shifts out of brain cells, causing confusion, seizures and coma. Correcting it too fast reverses the shift and risks cerebral oedema and osmotic demyelination.
Little ketosis: residual insulin suppresses lipolysis, so pH and bicarbonate are usually near normal (pH at least 7.3, bicarbonate at least 15).
Prothrombotic state: dehydration and hyperviscosity raise the risk of arterial and venous thrombosis.
Mortality is about ten times that of DKA (MOH: up to 20%); age, degree of dehydration and comorbidity drive prognosis.

symptoms: Develops over days to a week, usually in older adults with type 2 diabetes (can be the first presentation).
Polyuria, polydipsia, weight loss, weakness, vomiting.
Drowsiness, confusion, seizures or coma; focal neurological signs can occur.
Often co-presents with another acute illness (infection, MI, stroke).
physicalSigns: Severe dehydration: dry mucosa, poor skin turgor, tachycardia, hypotension.
Reduced GCS; no Kussmaul breathing (no significant acidosis).
Feet: check for ulcers and pressure areas; these patients are at very high risk of heel ulceration.
Signs of the precipitant: chest, urine, skin infection; stroke; MI.
redFlags: Systolic BP below 90 mmHg: resuscitate first; the SDCPG order sheet does not apply until SBP is at least 90
Falling GCS, seizures or new focal signs, especially during treatment: think cerebral oedema or stroke; consider CT brain
Osmolality falling more than 8 mOsm/kg/h or sodium falling more than 10 mmol/L in 24 h
Signs of limb ischaemia, DVT, PE or stroke (thrombosis)
precipitants: Infection (30–60%; pneumonia and urinary tract infection most common).
High-dose steroids and other drugs that raise glucose.
Poor adherence; impaired thirst or limited access to water (frail elderly).

differentials.distinguishingFeatures: Ketones at least 3.0 mmol/L with pH below 7.3 or bicarbonate below 18. Onset hours to days, Kussmaul breathing.
Hyperosmolar AND ketotic (ketones at least 3.0, urine ketones 2+ or more, pH below 7.30 or bicarbonate below 18): start insulin at 0.1 unit/kg/h (consensus) and correct osmolality slowly.
Focal signs, fever or neck stiffness out of proportion to the metabolic picture; confusion that does not improve as osmolality falls.
Glucose not markedly raised; osmolality driven by sodium.

ruleIn.clinicalRationale: Target a fall of no more than 5 mmol/L/h. Aim for 10–15 mmol/L in the first 24 h. Change to 5% dextrose in 0.9% NaCl when glucose is below 13 mmol/L.

ruleIn.testName: Serum osmolality (measured, or 2 × Na + glucose + urea)
ruleIn.modalityTarget: 0, 3, 6, 12 h, then every 12 h (SDCPG); every 4 h (consensus)
ruleIn.expectedFinding: Total above 320 mOsm/kg (SDCPG; consensus also accepts effective osmolality 2×Na + glucose above 300).
ruleIn.clinicalRationale: The key treatment target. Lower by about 5 mOsm/kg/h (consensus 3–8). Falling faster: cut fluid rate by 50%. Not falling despite positive balance, or corrected Na above 150: switch to 0.45% NaCl.

ruleIn.expectedFinding: Often normal or high; rises at first as glucose falls.
ruleIn.clinicalRationale: A rise in sodium as glucose falls is expected and is not a reason for hypotonic fluid while osmolality is falling. Sodium must not fall more than 10 mmol/L in 24 h.

clinicalManagement.title: Resuscitate and decide level of care
actions: ABC, cardiac monitor, urinary catheter if needed, foot examination.
SBP below 90: give 0.9% NaCl until SBP is at least 90, then follow the HHS protocol.
Most patients need HDU/ICU-level monitoring; start prophylactic LMWH unless contraindicated.

branches.condition: Ketones at least 3.0 or pH below 7.3
actions: Mixed DKA–HHS: start insulin now (consensus 0.1 unit/kg/h); otherwise follow this pathway.

clinicalManagement.title: Fluids are the main treatment
actions: 0.9% NaCl 1 L over the first hour (no potassium).
Then 0.9% NaCl 250 mL/h with potassium as per the algorithm (about 3 L over the next 11–12 h); aim to replace 4 L in the first 12 h.
Targets: positive balance 2–3 L by 6 h and 3–6 L by 12 h; replace the rest over the next 12 h. Rate not to exceed 250 mL/h on the order sheet.
Elderly, cardiac or renal patients: smaller volumes and frequent review.
Reduce the IV fluid rate by 50%.

branches.condition: Osmolality not falling despite positive balance, or corrected Na above 150
actions: Change to 0.45% NaCl at the same rate.
Change to 5% dextrose in 0.9% NaCl and halve insulin (see below).

clinicalManagement.title: Insulin: late and low
clinicalManagement.timeframe: Only after at least 1 L of fluid
actions: Fluid alone lowers glucose a lot in HHS. SDCPG: start insulin only after at least 1 L of fluid and if glucose is not falling, fluid balance is already positive, or there is significant ketosis.
Fixed rate 0.05 unit/kg/h (50 units in 50 mL 0.9% NaCl); never more than 0.05 unit/kg/h (e.g. 4 units/h in 80 kg).
Glucose below 13 mmol/L: reduce to 0.025 unit/kg/h. Glucose 5 mmol/L or less: add 10% dextrose at 50–100 mL/h; do not stop insulin.
Aim for glucose 10–15 mmol/L; fall no faster than 5 mmol/L/h.
Hold insulin for 2 h or until K is at least 3.3; replace potassium (40 mmol in 500 mL over 4 h, max 10 mmol/h).

clinicalManagement.title: Prevent complications
actions: Thromboprophylaxis with LMWH for all unless contraindicated; SDCPG suggests considering full anticoagulation.
Heel protectors and daily foot checks in neuropathy, deformity or vascular disease.
Treat the precipitant; antibiotics when infection is shown.

clinicalManagement.title: Recovery and transition
actions: Correction usually takes longer than 24 h; do not chase normal values quickly.
Consensus resolution: osmolality below 300 mOsm/kg, urine output above 0.5 mL/kg/h, cognition improved, glucose below 13.9 mmol/L.
Stop IV insulin once eating and drinking; most need subcutaneous insulin; some newly diagnosed or previously well-controlled patients can later go back to oral agents.
All patients see a diabetes educator.

keyPoints: Fluids first, insulin late and low (0.05 unit/kg/h).
Correct slowly: osmolality about 5 mOsm/kg/h, sodium no more than 10 mmol/L per 24 h, glucose no more than 5 mmol/L/h.
Rising sodium while osmolality falls is expected.
Thromboprophylaxis and heel protection for everyone.
pitfalls: Starting insulin before fluids: circulatory collapse.
Using DKA insulin doses (0.1 unit/kg/h) in pure HHS.
Switching to hypotonic fluid just because sodium rises.
Correcting too fast: cerebral oedema and osmotic demyelination.
Forgetting foot protection and VTE prophylaxis.

lifestyleAndDiet: Not applicable in the acute phase.
mdtReferrals: Geriatric or rehabilitation review if function declined.
dischargeCriteria: Osmolality, sodium and glucose improving and stable; eating and drinking.
Insulin or oral regimen established and taught.
nonClinicalManagement.followUpPlan: Diabetes clinic review early after discharge; recovery depends largely on prior functional status.

Ketones below 3.0 mmol/L or urine ketones below 2+; pH at least 7.3 and bicarbonate above 15 mmol/L

regimens.dose: 1 L over 1 h; then 250 mL/h for about 12 h; then 100–250 mL/h
regimens.duration: Replace about 4 L in 12 h; remainder over the next 12 h
adjustments: Halve the rate if osmolality falls more than 5 mOsm/kg/h
Switch to 0.45% NaCl if osmolality is not falling or corrected Na above 150

regimens.indication: Glucose control (after at least 1 L fluid)
regimens.dose: 0.05 unit/kg/h if glucose at least 13; 0.025 unit/kg/h if glucose below 13; maximum 0.05 unit/kg/h
monitoring: Hourly capillary glucose; aim 10–15 mmol/L, fall no more than 5 mmol/L/h

regimens.dose: K above 5.2: none; 3.3–5.2: 20–40 mmol/L; below 3.3: 40 mmol in 500 mL over 4 h
monitoring: ECG and cardiac monitor if below 3.3

regimens.patientGroup: Glucose below 13 mmol/L (5% dextrose) or 5 mmol/L or less (10%)
regimens.dose: D5/0.9% NaCl at the same rate; D10 at 50–100 mL/h until glucose reaches 10
